subject: Cognitive Science
title: Base Rate Thinking
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Base Rate Thinking.

hook.text: A test is 99% accurate. You test positive. What's the chance you're actually sick? Most people say 99%. They're wrong.

buildup.text: If the disease affects 1 in 10,000, most positives are false. The base rate—how common the condition is—matters enormously.

discovery.text: Base rate neglect is our tendency to ignore background frequencies and focus only on the specific case.

twist.text: Even doctors fall for it. In one study, 45% of physicians got the base rate problem wrong.

climax.text: Thinking in natural frequencies—'1 in 10,000 people'—instead of percentages dramatically improves accuracy.

punchline.text: Always ask: how common is this in the first place?

details.summary: Base rate thinking means considering how common something is before evaluating specific evidence. Most people skip this step, focusing on vivid details instead. Doctors who forget that a disease is rare misinterpret positive tests. Base rate neglect is one of the most consequential cognitive biases.
details.whyItMatters: Base rate neglect distorts medical, legal, and financial decisions. Training yourself to ask how common is this first dramatically improves judgment accuracy.
takeaways: Base rates tell you how common something is before any evidence
People routinely neglect base rates when given case details
Asking how common is this is a powerful debiasing question

faq.question: What is a real-world example of base rate neglect?
faq.answer: A cab hit a pedestrian at night. A witness says the cab was blue. Blue cabs are 15 percent of all cabs. Most people say the cab was probably blue based on the witness. But given witness error rates, the base rate of green cabs makes green more likely despite the testimony.

faq.question: How can you train yourself to use base rates?
faq.answer: Before evaluating any specific evidence, force yourself to estimate the base rate. How common is this diagnosis? How often do startups in this sector succeed? Starting from the base rate and adjusting with evidence produces far more calibrated judgments than starting from the case details.
